part: C2 Proficiency · Writing Part 1 (essay on two texts)
title: Should Magic Be Taught to Everyone?
task: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer. Write 240–280 words.

texts.title: Text 1: A Gift for All
texts.text: Magic should no longer be the privilege of a gifted few. When spellcraft is confined to elite academies, the kingdom wastes the talents of thousands of children who never get the chance to discover their abilities. Universal teaching would not only uncover hidden potential but also demystify magic, making it less frightening to ordinary citizens.

texts.title: Text 2: The Weight of Power
texts.text: Teaching magic to everyone sounds generous, but power without wisdom is dangerous. Most children lack the patience required to master even simple charms safely, and a single careless spell can cause lasting harm. Resources would be better spent on training fewer students thoroughly, ensuring that those who wield magic understand the responsibility it carries.

points.label: Summarise Text 1 (talent is wasted; teach everyone)

model:
Both texts address whether magic should be taught to every child, yet they reach strikingly different conclusions.

The first text contends that restricting magical education to elite academies squanders the talent of countless children who are never given the opportunity to discover what they can do. Universal teaching, the writer argues, would reveal this hidden potential and, as a welcome side effect, make magic seem less threatening to the general population. This is a compelling point, not least because fear of the unknown has historically fuelled prejudice. However, the writer rather glosses over the practical question of how such teaching would be made safe.

This is precisely the concern of the second writer, who maintains that power in the hands of the immature is a recipe for disaster. Since most children lack the patience to learn even basic charms properly, it would be wiser to train fewer students in depth. The argument is persuasive insofar as safety must come first, but it rests on the questionable assumption that only a select few are capable of responsibility. Were that true, we would hardly allow teenagers to learn to drive.

Ultimately, I would contend that the two positions are less incompatible than they appear. Rather than choosing between universal access and rigorous training, the kingdom could offer every child a foundation course focused on safety and ethics, reserving advanced study for those who demonstrate both aptitude and maturity. In this way, talent would be discovered without being recklessly unleashed, and responsibility would be taught as a core part of magic itself rather than as an afterthought.

part: C2 Proficiency · Writing Part 1 (essay on two texts)
title: The Value of Failure
task: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer. Write 240–280 words.

texts.title: Text 1: Fall Seven Times
texts.text: Every great knight has fallen from a horse. Failure is not the opposite of success but its apprenticeship: it exposes our weaknesses, builds resilience and teaches lessons that no triumph ever could. Schools that shield pupils from failure produce young people who crumble at the first setback.

texts.title: Text 2: In Praise of Getting It Right
texts.text: The fashionable celebration of failure has gone too far. Failing is often simply painful and discouraging, and repeated failure can convince young people that they are incapable. Rather than romanticising mistakes, we should design learning so that pupils experience frequent, well-earned success, which is what truly builds confidence.

model:
The two texts take opposing views on the role that failure should play in education, although, on closer inspection, they share more common ground than first appears.

The first writer maintains that failure is an essential stage on the road to success. Setbacks, it is argued, reveal our shortcomings and develop the resilience that achievement alone cannot provide, so pupils who are protected from failure will struggle to cope with adult life. The image of the fallen knight is memorable, and the underlying point is valid: anyone who has learnt a skill knows that mistakes are unavoidable.

The second text, however, takes issue with what it sees as a romantic glorification of failure. Its author points out that repeated failure is more likely to crush a learner's self-belief than to strengthen it, and that confidence is actually built through regular, deserved success. This is a persuasive corrective, particularly for struggling pupils, for whom yet another failure is hardly an inspiring lesson.

Be that as it may, the second writer arguably oversimplifies the first text, which never suggests that failure should be pursued for its own sake. What both writers would no doubt agree on is that the experience of failure matters less than how it is handled.

On balance, it seems to me that the most effective classrooms combine the two insights. Tasks should be pitched so that success is usually within reach, yet pupils should also be given safe opportunities to fail and, crucially, guidance on how to learn from it. Failure, in other words, is valuable only when it is followed by a way forward.

part: C2 Proficiency · Writing Part 1 (essay on two texts)
title: Libraries in the Digital Age
task: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer. Write 240–280 words.

texts.title: Text 1: Dusty Shelves
texts.text: Public libraries are relics of a world without the internet. Almost any book can now be downloaded in seconds, and maintaining vast buildings full of paper is an expensive indulgence. The money would be better invested in digital resources that every citizen can access from home.

texts.title: Text 2: More Than Books
texts.text: To judge libraries purely by their books is to misunderstand them. They are among the last public spaces where anyone may stay without spending money: a warm refuge for the lonely, a study room for students without quiet homes and a place where those without technology can still get online.

model:
The question of whether public libraries still have a place in a digital society divides the two writers sharply.

The first text dismisses libraries as outdated institutions, arguing that since books can now be downloaded almost instantly, it makes little financial sense to maintain enormous buildings filled with paper. Public money, the writer suggests, should instead be spent on digital collections accessible from anyone's home. The argument has a certain economic logic, yet it rests on the assumption that every citizen has a reliable device and internet connection, which is far from the case.

It is precisely this oversight that the second writer exposes. By contrast with the first text, it contends that a library's true value lies not in its shelves but in its function as one of the few remaining public spaces where nobody is required to spend money. Libraries offer shelter to isolated people, a quiet place to study for those who lack one and free access to technology for those who cannot afford it. This is, in my view, the more convincing analysis, because it considers who actually uses libraries rather than who could theoretically do without them.

That said, the first writer is right that libraries cannot remain unchanged. A library that ignores the digital revolution will struggle to justify its funding.

Ultimately, I would contend that the choice between paper and pixels is a false one. The most successful libraries are already becoming community hubs that lend e-books as well as novels, run digital skills classes and host local events. Far from being relics, such libraries may prove more necessary than ever in an increasingly isolated world.

title: Letter to the Starlight Library Board
task: The board of the Starlight Library plans to sell its collection of rare dragon manuscripts to a private collector to pay for repairs. Write a letter to the board objecting to the sale, acknowledging the financial pressures and proposing an alternative. Write 240–280 words.

points.label: Explain why the sale is wrong

model:
Dear Members of the Board,

I write to express my deep concern at the proposal to sell the library's collection of dragon manuscripts to a private buyer. Having consulted these documents for my own research over many years, I am convinced that their sale would be an irreversible mistake.

Whilst I fully appreciate the financial pressures the library faces, and I recognise that the roof repairs cannot be postponed indefinitely, the manuscripts are not merely assets to be traded. They are the only surviving record of the dragon dialects, and scholars from across the continent travel here specifically to study them. Were they to disappear into a private collection, public access would almost certainly be lost for generations, and with it a significant part of our shared heritage.

Moreover, the sale would set a troubling precedent. If the board is prepared to part with its rarest treasures to solve one crisis, what is to prevent the same reasoning being applied the next time funds run short?

I would therefore like to propose an alternative. Rather than selling the collection, the library could launch a public appeal, offering supporters the chance to sponsor the conservation of individual manuscripts. A touring exhibition of high-quality facsimiles could also generate considerable income while the originals remain safely at home. Should the board wish to explore these ideas, I would be glad to help draft a funding application to the Royal Heritage Trust.

I urge you to reconsider before a decision is made that cannot be undone.

Yours faithfully,
Dr Imogen Vale

title: Review: An Evening at the Dragon Opera
task: An arts magazine has invited readers to review a live performance they attended recently. Write a review evaluating the production, comparing it with your expectations and saying which audiences it would suit. Write 240–280 words.
model:
Fire and Feeling: The Dragon's Lament

I confess that I arrived at the Starlight Opera House expecting little more than an expensive spectacle. The Dragon's Lament had been marketed almost entirely on its special effects, and I had assumed that the music would play second fiddle to the pyrotechnics. Rarely have I been so pleased to be proved wrong.

The production tells the story of an ageing dragon who must decide whether to surrender her hoard to save the city that despises her. What lingers in the memory is not the fire, impressive as it is, but the extraordinary performance of Mara Kell in the title role. Her voice moves effortlessly from a menacing growl to a fragile whisper, and her final aria, sung almost motionless in a single shaft of light, left much of the audience in tears.

The staging is equally remarkable. Rather than relying on a mechanical dragon, the director uses twelve dancers in shimmering costumes who together form the creature's body, a device that is both ingenious and strangely moving.

If anything, the production falters only in its second act, where a subplot involving two squabbling knights adds comic relief, albeit at the expense of momentum. The score, too, occasionally borrows rather too obviously from more famous works.

These are minor reservations, however. The opera surpassed my expectations in every way that matters, and it deserves to be remembered for its heart rather than its flames. Seasoned opera lovers will find much to admire, while those who have never set foot in an opera house could hardly hope for a more captivating introduction. It is not to be missed.

title: The Lost Art of Doing Nothing
task: A magazine is publishing a series on modern life. Write an article entitled “The Lost Art of Doing Nothing”, explaining why people find it so hard to be idle, what we lose as a result and how readers might rediscover the value of doing nothing. Write 240–280 words.
model:
The Lost Art of Doing Nothing

When did you last sit on a bench and simply watch the clouds drift by, without reaching for your phone? If you cannot remember, you are in good company. Doing nothing has become one of the rarest activities of modern life.

It is not that we lack free moments, but rather that we have learnt to fill every one of them. Waiting for a bus, queuing for coffee, even lying in bed, we scroll, check and reply. Behind this constant activity lies a quiet sense of guilt: in a culture that measures our worth by our productivity, an idle hour feels like a small moral failure.

Little do we realise how much this costs us. Psychologists have long observed that the wandering mind is far from inactive; it is in moments of apparent idleness that the brain connects distant ideas, processes experiences and stumbles upon creative solutions. Paradoxically, the people who never stop working may be depriving themselves of their best ideas. Our wellbeing suffers too, since a mind that is never allowed to rest can never fully recharge.

Rediscovering the art of doing nothing does not require a retreat to a mountain monastery. Start by setting aside ten minutes a day with no screen, no task and no goal. Resist the urge to call it meditation or to measure its benefits, which would only turn it into another chore. Simply sit, look and let your thoughts go wherever they please.

So the next time you find yourself with an empty moment, consider leaving it empty. You may be surprised by what fills it.

part: C2 Proficiency · Writing Part 1 (essay on two texts)
title: Should Zoos Still Exist?
task: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer. Write 240–280 words.

texts.title: Text 1: A Safe Harbour
texts.text: Well-run zoos have become vital lifeboats for endangered species. Breeding programmes have rescued animals such as the Arabian oryx from extinction, and the millions of children who visit each year develop a fondness for wildlife that no textbook could inspire. Closing zoos would abandon these animals at precisely the moment they need us most.

texts.title: Text 2: A Cage Is Still a Cage
texts.text: However spacious an enclosure may be, it can never replace the wild. Elephants, big cats and dolphins often show signs of stress in captivity, and only a small fraction of zoo animals belong to endangered species. The money spent on visitor attractions would achieve far more if it protected the habitats where animals actually live.

points.label: Summarise Text 1 (zoos save species and inspire children)
Summarise Text 2 (captivity harms animals; protect habitats)

model:
The two texts offer sharply contrasting answers to the question of whether zoos still deserve a place in the modern world.

The first text contends that well-managed zoos act as a last refuge for species on the brink of extinction. Breeding schemes, the writer points out, have already brought animals such as the Arabian oryx back from the edge, while the sight of a living tiger can awaken a lifelong love of nature in a child far more effectively than any book. This is a compelling argument, not least because conservation depends on public support. However, it rather overlooks the welfare of the individual animals involved.

It is precisely this issue that the second writer raises. Even the most generous enclosure, the text maintains, is a poor substitute for the wild, and many large mammals display clear signs of distress in captivity. Moreover, since most zoo animals are not endangered at all, the conservation argument applies to only a small fraction of them. The suggestion that funds would be better spent protecting natural habitats is persuasive, yet it underestimates how many habitats have already been destroyed beyond repair.

Ultimately, I would contend that both writers are partly right. Were zoos to disappear overnight, several species would vanish with them; on the other hand, keeping animals simply to entertain visitors is increasingly difficult to justify. It is therefore essential that every zoo be judged by a single standard: whether it genuinely contributes to protecting animals in the wild. Those that do deserve our support, whereas those that do not should, arguably, close their gates for good.

part: C2 Proficiency · Writing Part 1 (essay on two texts)
title: Winning, Losing and School Sport
task: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer. Write 240–280 words.

texts.title: Text 1: The Thrill of the Race
texts.text: Competition is what makes sport exciting. Striving to beat a rival teaches young people to set goals, train hard and cope with disappointment, lessons that will serve them well long after they leave school. A sports day without winners would not protect children; it would simply deny the talented a chance to shine.

texts.title: Text 2: Everyone on the Pitch
texts.text: School sport too often rewards the few at the expense of the many. Pupils who are always picked last soon decide that exercise is not for them, and some give it up entirely. Schools should value effort, enjoyment and improvement, so that every child, however skilled, leaves with a love of being active.

points.label: Summarise Text 2 (it puts many pupils off; value effort)

model:
Few questions divide teachers and parents quite as reliably as the role of competition in school sport, and the two texts take markedly different positions on it.

The first writer maintains that the desire to beat a rival is the very essence of sport. Competing, it is argued, teaches young people to set goals, to train with determination and to recover from defeat, all of which are valuable well beyond the playing field. Removing winners, the writer adds, would merely hold back the most talented pupils. There is a good deal of truth in this, since many athletes trace their motivation back to a single race at school.

The second text, however, takes issue with a system that celebrates a gifted minority. Its author observes that children who are repeatedly picked last tend to conclude that exercise is not for them, and that some abandon it altogether. Rather than prizes for the fastest, schools should reward effort, enjoyment and personal improvement. This is a persuasive point, particularly at a time when so many young people lead inactive lives.

Be that as it may, the second writer arguably oversimplifies the first, which never suggests that only winners matter. Both writers would no doubt agree that the purpose of school sport is to produce adults who stay active.

On balance, it seems to me that the two approaches can coexist. Schools could offer competitive leagues for those who relish them alongside non-competitive activities such as climbing or dance. It is vital that no pupil leave school believing that sport belongs only to the fortunate few.

title: Why We Should All Look Up
task: A science magazine for young people is publishing a series called “Wonders on Your Doorstep”. Write an article entitled “Why We Should All Look Up”, explaining why so few people notice the night sky today, what we miss as a result and how readers could start stargazing. Write 240–280 words.

points.label: Why few people notice the night sky
What we miss as a result

model:
Why We Should All Look Up

When did you last stop on a clear night and simply gaze at the stars? For most of us, the answer is probably “not for ages”, and the reason is not hard to find.

It is not that the stars have disappeared, but rather that we have hidden them. In towns and cities, the orange glow of street lights, known as light pollution, washes out all but the brightest points in the sky. Even when we are somewhere truly dark, our eyes are usually fixed on a screen, and the sky above passes unnoticed.

Little do we realise how much we lose as a result. For thousands of years, the night sky was a storybook, a calendar and a map: sailors steered by it, farmers planted by it and every culture filled it with heroes and animals. Paradoxically, although we now know more about space than ever before, far fewer people have actually seen the Milky Way with their own eyes. That sense of awe, the feeling of being a tiny part of something unimaginably vast, is a powerful spark for curiosity, and it is a great pity to miss it.

Fortunately, rediscovering the stars is remarkably easy. Start by finding the darkest spot you can, perhaps a park or a back garden, and give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust. A free star-map app will help you spot the constellations, and a simple pair of binoculars will reveal the craters of the Moon.

So the next time the sky is clear, why not switch off your screen and look up? You may be astonished by what has been there all along.

title: Report: The Inter-School Robot Challenge
task: Your school sent a team to an inter-school robot challenge, and the organisers have asked participants for feedback. Write a report evaluating the event, explaining what could be improved and recommending whether your school should take part again next year. Write 240–280 words.

points.label: Recommend whether to take part again

model:
Purpose
This report sets out to evaluate the Inter-School Robot Challenge held at Riverside Academy last month, drawing on the views of our six team members and their teacher, and to recommend whether the school should enter again.

Strengths of the event
By any measure, the challenge was a remarkable success. Twenty-four teams took part, each required to build a robot capable of sorting coloured blocks and navigating a miniature obstacle course. What participants valued most was the workshop on the opening morning, in which engineers from a local company offered practical advice on sensors and coding. The atmosphere, moreover, was supportive rather than fiercely competitive: rival teams regularly lent each other spare parts and tools.

Areas for improvement
Nevertheless, a number of shortcomings were noted. The timetable was extremely tight, so several teams had barely an hour to repair robots damaged in the early rounds. In addition, the judging criteria were published only on the day itself, which left some groups feeling that their designs had been built for the wrong task. Arguably, the event would also have benefited from a quiet area, since the main hall was so noisy that team members could scarcely hear one another.

Recommendations
Were the organisers to publish the rules a month in advance and allow longer repair breaks, most of these problems would disappear. As for our own participation, the experience developed our team's problem-solving skills and confidence to a degree that ordinary lessons rarely achieve. It is therefore strongly recommended that the school take part again next year, ideally with a second team so that more students can benefit.
